---
title: "Archetypal analysis, visually"
description: "A gentle, visual introduction to archetypal analysis: describing data as mixtures of a few extreme cases."
bibliography: references.bib
link-citations: true
---

Think of a paint shop. It does not sell thousands of colours: it sells a few pure ones, and every other colour is a mix of them. **Archetypal analysis** (AA) does the same with data. It looks for a handful of extreme, "pure" cases, the **archetypes**, and describes everything else as a mixture of them.

Instead of asking *"which group does this belong to?"*, it asks *"how much of each extreme does this have?"* No maths is needed to follow the ideas below; the formulas are at the end for the curious.





## A cloud of athletes

Imagine we measured 150 athletes and drew each one as a dot. Athletes who are alike end up close together. (In statistics, each athlete is one **observation**.)

To be able to draw them, each athlete is described here by just two numbers. Real data usually have many more, dozens or even thousands of measurements, but the ideas below are exactly the same; we just cannot draw them. (The data here are made up, just to have something to look at.)

::: {#26bfbfb7 .cell execution_count=3}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![150 athletes, one dot each. Similar athletes are close together.](archetypal-analysis_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.svg){fig-alt='A cloud of grey dots with a roughly triangular shape.'}
:::
:::


Look at the shape of the cloud: it sticks out in three directions. Near the tip of each one live athletes who are extreme in some way: very fast over a short distance, very enduring, very strong. Let us give those tips names.

::: {#c4110983 .cell execution_count=4}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![The three archetypes: the extreme cases at the tips of the cloud. The triangle they form contains most athletes.](archetypal-analysis_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.svg){fig-alt='The same cloud, with a coloured dot at each tip labelled Sprinter, Marathoner and Weightlifter, joined by a triangle.'}
:::
:::


Nobody has to be exactly a sprinter, a marathoner or a weightlifter. A decathlete, for example, is a bit of all three. (Some athletes fall outside the triangle; we will get to them in a moment.) That is the whole idea: *the extremes are the building blocks, and every athlete is a mixture of them*.

## Every athlete is a mixture

To say how much of each archetype an athlete has, we use three percentages that add up to 100%. They are the athlete's **weights**. Watch one athlete walk around the triangle: the lines go to the archetypes, the bar chart shows the weights, and the dot takes the blend of the archetypes' colours that matches them.

::: {#7bf7405a .cell execution_count=5}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=75}
![One athlete moves through the triangle. The bars give the share of each archetype. At an archetype the athlete is 100% that archetype; along an edge only two archetypes matter; in the middle there is a bit of everything. The closer to an archetype, the larger its share. The dot is coloured by the blend of the archetypes' colours given by its weights.](archetypal-analysis_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.svg){fig-alt='An animation of a dot moving inside the triangle of archetypes, with three bars showing how much of each archetype it contains.'}
:::
:::


## Athletes outside the triangle

Look at the cloud again: some athletes lie *outside* the triangle. A mixture of the archetypes can only land *inside* it, so these athletes cannot be written exactly as a mixture.

AA deals with them in the simplest possible way: each athlete is described by the **closest point of the triangle**, the mixture that looks most like them. Watch the athletes outside the triangle slide to their closest mixture. The thin line they leave behind is what the description gets wrong.

::: {#16d89502 .cell execution_count=6}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=76}
![Athletes outside the triangle (dark dots) are described by the closest mixture of the archetypes, on its edge. The line that joins each athlete to its description is the part that the archetypes fail to explain.](archetypal-analysis_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.svg){fig-alt='An animation in which the dark dots outside the triangle slide to the nearest point of its border, leaving a thin line behind, and then go back.'}
:::
:::


Two things follow from this. First, the leftover gap is exactly the **error** we will use later to find the archetypes and to decide how many we need. Second, since archetypes are built from real athletes, the triangle can never reach beyond the data: the most extreme athletes will usually be a little outside it. That is the price of keeping the archetypes realistic.

## Archetypes come from real data

There is a catch. If we were free to put the three archetypes anywhere, we could invent "athletes" that nobody has ever seen. AA avoids this with a second rule: **each archetype must itself be a mixture of real athletes**.

So archetypes are extreme, but never imaginary: they sit at the edge of the data, built from observations that actually exist. You can always go and look at the athletes behind an archetype, which makes the result easy to interpret. In the figure below, the zoom visits each archetype in turn.

::: {#ea31b02c .cell execution_count=7}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=77}
![An archetype is built from real observations. Left: the cloud, with the area being shown marked. Right: zoom into that area, which visits each archetype in turn. An archetype (large dot) is a weighted average of a few real athletes, joined to it by lines that are thicker the larger their weight. The Sprinter needs no lines: it coincides with a single real athlete.](archetypal-analysis_files/figure-html/cell-8-output-1.svg){fig-alt='An animation with two panels. The left one shows the cloud with a small dashed square that moves from one archetype to the next. The right one zooms into that square, where a large coloured dot, the archetype, is joined by lines of different thickness to a few real athletes.'}
:::
:::


## Archetypes are not averages

A more familiar way to summarise data is **clustering**: split the athletes into groups and describe each group by its average, the *centroid*. A centroid is the *typical* member of a group, so it lies in the middle of the cloud. An archetype is the opposite: the *extreme* member, on the edge.

The closest relative of AA is **fuzzy c-means**, a "soft" clustering method. Like AA, it gives every athlete percentages that add up to 100%, one for each group. But the percentages mean something different. In c-means they say *how close the athlete is to each typical case*. In AA they say *how much of each extreme the athlete is made of*.

::: {#93062b5d .cell execution_count=8}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Fuzzy c-means (left) and archetypal analysis (right) on the same athletes. Each dot is coloured by the blend of the colours of its three references, according to its percentages. c-means measures closeness to three typical cases, the squares, which sit inside the cloud. AA describes each athlete as a mixture of three extremes, the dots on the edge. The triangle of the centres leaves most athletes outside; the triangle of the archetypes covers most of them.](archetypal-analysis_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.svg){fig-alt='Two panels with the same cloud. On the left, three squares inside the cloud, the centres found by fuzzy c-means. On the right, the three archetypes at the tips.'}
:::
:::


## How are archetypes found?

Nobody knows the archetypes in advance, so the computer finds them by trial and improvement:

1. **Guess.** Start with three random athletes as archetypes.
2. **Check.** Try to rebuild every athlete as a mixture of the archetypes. The gap between each athlete and its rebuilt version is the **error**. We report it as the share of the athletes' variation that is left unexplained, which is why the axis of the figure below says "unexplained variation".
3. **Improve.** Nudge the archetypes, and the weights, in the direction that makes the error smaller.
4. **Repeat** until the error stops improving.

At 0% unexplained variation the archetypes rebuild everyone perfectly; at 100% they do no better than describing everybody as "the average athlete". A bad first guess can be even worse than that, so the curve starts above 100%. Watch the archetypes (left) leave their random starting points and slide towards the tips while the unexplained variation (right) drops.

::: {#08f4e189 .cell execution_count=9}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=79}
![Fitting archetypes. Left: they start at three random athletes and move towards the extremes. Right: the unexplained variation drops quickly at first, then flattens out as the archetypes settle.](archetypal-analysis_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.svg){fig-alt='An animation of three coloured dots moving from the middle of a cloud to its tips, next to a curve of the unexplained variation going down.'}
:::
:::


## How many archetypes?

We have used three because that is what this cloud looks like. With real data we have to choose. Too few archetypes cannot describe the data well; too many make the description longer and harder to read, and eventually they stop being "extreme" and start to pick up individual odd athletes.

A common recipe is to try several values and watch how much variation is left unexplained.

::: {#7852f46c .cell execution_count=10}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![The same athletes described with 2, 3, 4 and 5 archetypes. With two, the line cannot reach most of the cloud (a lot of variation is left unexplained). With three, the triangle covers most athletes. Beyond that, the extra archetypes barely help.](archetypal-analysis_files/figure-html/cell-11-output-1.svg){fig-alt='Four panels with the same cloud and different numbers of archetypes, each with the unexplained variation below.'}
:::
:::


Plotting the final unexplained variation against the number of archetypes makes the choice easier. We look for the **elbow**: the point after which adding archetypes stops paying off.

::: {#0d55b569 .cell execution_count=11}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Unexplained variation against the number of archetypes. It falls sharply up to three archetypes and hardly changes afterwards: the elbow is at three. In real data the elbow is rarely this sharp, so the choice also depends on what you want to interpret.](archetypal-analysis_files/figure-html/cell-12-output-1.svg){fig-alt='A line chart of the unexplained variation against the number of archetypes, dropping steeply until three and flat afterwards.'}
:::
:::


## Where is it useful?

AA shines whenever the extremes tell you more than the averages. It was introduced by Adele Cutler and Leo Breiman [-@cutler1994], and it fits questions like these:

- **Describing people or objects by a few extreme profiles**, such as body shapes, player styles or customer types, instead of forcing everyone into a single group.
- **Finding the extreme situations in data**, such as unusual weather patterns, rather than their averages.

## Things to keep in mind

- **Outliers matter.** Archetypes live at the extremes, so a few very unusual observations can pull them. It is worth looking at the data first.
- **The answer is not unique.** Different starting guesses can end in slightly different archetypes. Here we tried four starts and kept the best.
- **Choosing the number of archetypes is a judgement.** The elbow helps, but what you want to interpret matters too.
- **Scales matter.** If the variables are in very different units, the largest ones dominate, so they are usually put on a comparable scale first.

## In short

- **Archetypes** are a few extreme cases that summarise a dataset.
- Every observation is a **mixture** of them: percentages that add up to 100%.
- Archetypes are built from **real observations**, so they are extreme but realistic.
- They are different from **averages**: archetypes sit on the edge of the data, centroids in the middle.
- The computer finds them by **trial and improvement**, and we choose how many to use by watching the **unexplained variation**.
- They are sensitive to **outliers**, and the solution is not unique, so look at the data first.

## The maths, for the curious

Put the $n$ observations, each described by $p$ numbers, in a matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$, and the $k$ archetypes in the rows of $Z \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times p}$. The weights of each observation form a matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}$, and the data are approximated by

$$
X \approx A Z .
$$

The second rule, that archetypes are mixtures of real observations, reads $Z = B X$, where $B \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times n}$ holds the weights. Fitting the model means solving

$$
\min_{A,\,B}\ \lVert X - A B X \rVert_F^2
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad A\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1},\ B\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1},\ A, B \ge 0 .
$$

$A$ says how much of each archetype every observation has; $B$ says which observations each archetype is made of. The constraints are exactly the two rules above: every row of weights is non-negative and adds up to one, so every mixture is an average. The unexplained variation shown in the figures is $\lVert X - ABX\rVert_F^2$ divided by the total variation of the data, $\lVert X - \bar{X}\rVert_F^2$, that is, $1 - R^2$. Distances are squared, so a value of 3% corresponds to a typical gap of about $\sqrt{0.03} \approx 17\%$ of the spread of the data.
